analysis.one_liner: Makes the corporate research tax credit permanent and boosts it for companies producing mainly in the U.S.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a vote or any action after its April 2011 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The research tax credit has long been a 'temporary' credit that Congress has to keep renewing. This bill would have made it permanent, so companies could count on it every year, and would have added up to 10 extra percentage points to the credit for companies earning more than half their money from production done in the United States. The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that spend on research and development — especially large pharmaceutical, technology, and manufacturing firms — would get a permanent tax credit they could count on, and companies with most of their production in the U.S. would get a credit worth up to 10 percentage points more. Business groups have long argued the on-again, off-again renewal cycle makes the credit less effective at encouraging research planning.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the research tax credit permanent by repealing its expiration date, so companies no longer have to wait on Congress to renew it.
Adds 2 to 10 percentage points to the credit rate for companies that earn more than half their gross receipts from domestic production activities.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and ultimately taxpayers — would bear the cost of a permanent, larger research credit. Since the credit expires regularly, taxpayers already implicitly pay for it in repeated extensions; this bill would lock in that cost with no expiration and add a bonus on top.

drawbacks.text: Making the credit permanent converts a recurring 'temporary' tax break — one Congress typically reviews and renews every year or two — into a permanent reduction in federal revenue with no offset, adding to deficits.

The extra credit boost for companies with majority-domestic production receipts adds further cost to the Treasury, and the mechanism rewards companies based on how they report domestic production receipts, a definition that benefits large manufacturers most.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — permanence for the R&D credit — would give businesses certainty to plan long-term research, a goal with bipartisan support that Congress has since embraced. The cost is roughly $10 billion or more per year in foregone federal revenue, borne by the general taxpayer, with the extra bonus stacked on top for domestic manufacturers. The bill never advanced far enough for its design details to be debated, and it was written as a pure tax cut with no offsetting revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Leonard Lance introduced the bill on April 1, 2011, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup, the House never voted, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

The bill would have repealed the expiration date on the research credit (Section 41(h) of the tax code) and added a 2-to-10 percentage-point bonus to the credit for taxpayers with more than half their gross receipts from domestic production activities.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and taxpayers were spared the cost of a permanent, larger research credit, and no one had to fight for the bill's defeat — it simply never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, who avoided a permanent new tax cut

for.name: Rep. Leonard Lance
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the research credit permanent and expanded it for domestic producers.

for.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or advanced it, letting it die.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and it never advanced far enough for a party-line fight to emerge.

industries.note: A permanent research credit plus a bonus of up to 10 percentage points for companies doing most of their production in the U.S. means a larger, guaranteed annual tax cut. The credit's value flows primarily to large firms with substantial research budgets.
The bill ties the extra credit to the section 199 'domestic production' definition, channeling the largest increases to manufacturers producing in the United States.
